nameStory: The 'notched' in this brittle star's name comes from the distinctive notches or indentations along the edges of its central disk where the five arms attach. Brittle stars get their name because their long, slender arms break off easily when grabbed by predators - a clever escape trick that lets them scurry away while the predator is left holding just an arm that will eventually regrow.
description: The Notched Brittle Star is a fascinating sea creature that looks like a small, flat star with five extremely long, snake-like arms extending from a round central disk. The central disk is typically about half an inch across, while the flexible arms can stretch out to make the entire animal span 3-4 inches from arm tip to arm tip. Unlike sea stars, brittle stars move by rapidly wriggling their arms in a swimming motion rather than crawling on tube feet, and their arms are clearly distinct from their central body.

idTips.label: Notched disk edges
idTips.description: The central disk has distinctive V-shaped notches where each arm meets the body, giving it a scalloped appearance rather than a smooth round edge

idTips.label: Arm flexibility
idTips.description: Arms are extremely flexible and snake-like, able to coil and twist in ways that would be impossible for a sea star's rigid arms

idTips.label: Disk texture
idTips.description: Central disk feels smooth and slightly leathery to gentle touch, covered in small overlapping scales that give it a subtle bumpy texture

idTips.label: Arm banding
idTips.description: Arms often show alternating light and dark bands or mottled patterns, with a slightly rougher texture than the smooth central disk

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: When disturbed, moves with rapid, writhing motions of the arms, quite different from the slow gliding of sea stars

habitat: Found in deeper waters off New England's coast, typically on sandy or muddy bottoms from about 30 feet down to several hundred feet deep. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often hide under rocks, shells, or in crevices during the day. You're most likely to encounter them if you're scuba diving or find one washed up after storms on beaches with nearby deep water access.

seasonality.spring: Active in deeper waters as water temperatures begin to warm, though rarely visible to shore-based observers.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with peak feeding behavior, but still primarily in offshore deeper waters beyond typical swimming depths.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity may occasionally wash specimens onto beaches, particularly after strong offshore storms or hurricanes.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water, remaining hidden in crevices and under cover on the sea floor.

funFact: When a brittle star loses an arm to a predator, it doesn't just regrow the missing limb - the severed arm can actually continue moving on its own for several minutes, writhing and twisting to distract the predator while the rest of the animal escapes to safety!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other brittle star species, but the distinctive notches where arms meet the central disk are unique to this species. Remember: 'Notched edges, Notched name' - if the disk edge is smooth where arms attach, it's a different brittle star species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'brittle star,' these animals are actually more closely related to sea urchins than to true sea stars, and they belong to a completely different group called ophiuroids. The scientific name 'Ophiura' literally means 'snake-tail,' referring to their serpentine arm movements.
compareHints: This is the primary Ophiura species found in New England waters, distinguished from other brittle star genera by its relatively large, robust central disk and the characteristic notching pattern. Other brittle stars in New England waters typically have smoother disk edges, different arm-to-disk size ratios, or more delicate overall construction.
